(a) bilinguals' category-good ratings are affected by language mode (b) bilinguals' discrimination performance is unaffected by language mode (c) bilinguals' categorization and discrimination performance is biased toward their dominant (English) language.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
bilinguals integrate their two languages in a common perceptual space, but they selectively attend to the language-specific phonetic details that are relevant to phonologically motivated judgments.

the two phonological systems of bilinguals are integrated in a single phonetic space, and that the perceptual patterns of the bilinguals reflect the language environment of the long-term dominant language.

the bilinguals' phonetic representations of a given phoneme are not completely language-specific but rather language-dominant, and this language dominance affects their perception in a language-specific way.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the phonetic space for bilinguals is not a simple combination of the two languages' phonetic spaces.
the phonetic space is common for both languages and is biased toward the L2-dominance of the bilinguals.
the bilingual's two language systems are integrated in perception, yet they are not equally available for all tasks.
The main takeaway from our work is that
bilinguals' perceptual patterns for a given phonetic contrast are not determined by their current language mode.
bilinguals' phonological systems are not completely integrated or completely separate, but rather are integrated with language-specific constraints.
the phonetic space of a bilingual is not a simple average of the phonetic spaces for the languages in their repertoire, as is often assumed.
